items.body: As I already had the privilege to write a feature about the posthumously released album Stellar Regions on this blog, i want to stretch this even a bit further. Here, I take a look at the period to follow, which eventually and fatally turned out to be the last five months in John Coltrane’s life. My focus is on the production of music in this final stage, as far it has been recorded and released, rather than John’s personal or health condition. On 15 February 1967, John had recorded the tracks eventually released as Stellar Regions in 1995 (see my earlier feature) with the quartet. One week later, on 22 February 1967, he returned with Rashied Ali for a saxophone – drums duo session, eventually to be released as Interstellar Space (see Gary Chapin‘s feature on this album). On 07 March 1967, in another session with the quartet again, he recorded two tracks, as far as we know, Ogunde and Number One . Ogunde is, first of all, a relatively short piece at a few seconds over 3 ½ minutes. A noticeable parallel to Stellar Regions , where the title track and Iris have approximately the same length and concise structure. The track takes its title presumably from an afro-brazilean folk song „Ogundu Varere“, rougly translated as a prayer to the gods. John occupied himself with spiritual traditions especially from Africa. John uses his forceful, cry-like late saxophone sound, overblowing his instrument, which gives an emotional urgence to the piece. The theme starts with a solemn, hmyn-like melody, but breaks out in free, atonal outbursts, before it fades away. In summary, John condenses the intensity of his (at that time) usually half-hour long live improvisations into less than a handful of minutes (but see below, what happened live). At some time in spring (David S. Wild confirmed in the liner notes for Stellar Regions that this track was not recorded on 15 February, so the actual recording date remains unknown), John must have recorded To Be , where he plays flute and is rejoined by Pharoah Sanders on piccolo flute. He shows a very calm, introspective and meditative side here. At over 16 minutes playing time, this track feels like a spiritual retreat. The two flutes give it an airy, almost floating mood. Alice Coltrane’s flowing piano style provides a mystic, harp-like cushion. Rashied Ali on drums and Jimmy Garrison on bass keep it calm and subdued. All together, the piece lacks a trditional jazz pulse, even leaves traditional jazz structures completely and makes a profound structural switch towards a meditative, open-end spiritual incantation. It stands as one of the most explicit artifacts of the creative partnership between John and Alice at that final stage and already mirrors the „cosmic jazz“ landscapes that Alice would pioneer on her own in the years to follow in her landmark solo releases ( Universal Consciousness , Journey in Satchidananda). Not to forget about Pharoah Sanders (Karma). Also unknown is the exact recording date for the piece titled Expression in spring 1967 with the quartet, which later lended its title to the album. 23 April 1967 is the date of the last live recording, The Olatunji Concert. This performance, originally recorded for a radio broadcast, is featured by Fotis Nikolakopoulos on this blog, so see there. With due respect to Fotis, I will limit myself here to the absolutely striking contrast between the live version of Ogunde and the studio version. Performed live, it swells to 28 minutes playing time. The studio recording’s tight and condensed structure is only preserved in the theme at the beginning to which it returns only at the very end. In between, it gets overwhelmed by a storm-like wave of pure energy. After the introduction of the melody as theme, the structure collapses completely in a ritual storm. A dense, polyrhythmic vortex is unchained in Rashied Ali’s drumming. Alice Coltrane plays cascade-like runs on the piano. On saxophone, Pharoah Sanders adds his bone-rattling, ecstatic overblowing cries. Yes, the quartet has been expanded here. Pharoah Sanders is back at it on the second saxophone. Two additional percussionists joined in, Algie DeWitt and Jumma Santos. The last ever live gig came at Baltimore’s Famous Ballroom on May 7, 1967. No audio recording of that performance is known to exist. On 17 May 1967, exactly two months before John’s death, a sextet met for a last studio recording. The master tapes have been lost or at least unissued so two tracks with the titles None Other and Kaleidoscope have been unreleased so far and do not even appear on retrospective compilations. With the recorded material, a last studio record was conceived during John’s lifetime. It was given the title Expression . John was actively involved in the production and met with Bob Thiele. On side 1, it had Ogunde as the opening track (the studio version, as above, of course). Track #2 was To Be with John and Pharoah Sanders on flutes (as above). At over 16 minutes, it was the longest track, making up for nearly half of the original album’s playing time, and the only track on the album in which Pharoah Sanders made an appearance. Side 2 opened with the majestic ballad Offering , the only track chosen from the 15 February session, thus making it the only track on the posthumous album Stellar Regions (see there) that had been released before and had an original title. Hank Shteamer has just featured this track prominently in the New York Times and put it into the larger context of spiritual jazz, for which a piece like Offering „would seem like a perfect prototype“ (Hank Shteamer, Spiritual Jazz Has Turned Cozy. John Coltrane Demanded More. New York Times, September 18, 2026). The original album closed with the title track Expression, John‘s last studio recording to ever be released. In the later CD release only, Number O ne, recorded on the same day as Ogunde , was added as a bonus track (the track, however, had been released for the first time in a 1978 compilation album). Obviously, the most recent recording session of May 1967 was not considered in the process at all (at that time, the tapes at least should still have been around, I guess?). John reportedly selected the four tracks for the original album release and their exact sequence himself. On Friday, 14 July 1967, three days before his death, he met Bob Thiele, handed the master tapes over to him and finally authorised the title and the release of the album, but expressed his opposition against liner notes. Expression , as John Coltrane’s final statement, was released in September 1967, two months after his death, containing John‘s chronologically last audible studio recordings and being the first posthumous release of his music. items.body: Over the past five years, Philip Samartzis has been building a body of distinct work. The interrelated recordings are identifiable by their adjacent titles: 2021’s Polar Force / Array (with Eugene Ughetti); 2023’s Atmospheres and Disturbances; 2024’s Air Pressure (with Michael Vorfeld); and now 2026’s Atmospheric Pressure, again with Vorfeld. The starting point for these ventures was a pair of residencies sponsored by the Australian Antarctic Territory Arts Fellowship program. Samartzis was able to capture some incredible recordings in sub-zero temperatures, and they have proven to be a wealth of material in both pure and sculpted forms. As on Air Pressure, Samartzis contributes electronics, Vorfeld stringed instruments and percussion. The new set zeroes in on a 36-hour blizzard at the Casey Research Station in 2016. Amid the hundred-knot winds and white-out conditions, “the station was reduced to pressure, vibration, and sound.” Simply picturing David Nielson’s cover image of David Ward inspecting dog lines in 1990, one can already feel the cold and intuit the level of difficulty. “Gravitational Overflow” sets the stage with slowly increasing winds and the creak of vanes (personified by Vorfeld’s instruments). The wind and snow create their own music, an undulating drone of literal white noise. Percussion enters as sympathetic partner; one imagines the rattling of glass and iron, caught in a maelstrom of Biblical proportions. Toward the end, these metallic pats and taps take center stage, as if representing the eye of the hurricane. “Depression” refers to atmospheric conditions, although one would be forgiven for thinking that it might mirror a mood. The isolation of research stations often produces feelings of malaise. The electronics and radio chatter are surprises in the wake of the opener; some portions even sound like turntable scratches or graffiti cans being shaken. The focus is not on the machine hum and motor sputter, but instead, what happens when the electricity fails. The purely percussive section arrives earlier, in the sixth minute, like the last sounds of a man caught in a storm, having lost all bearings, facing death by making music one last time, his only audience the abyss. “Cold Front” reveals the full depth of the danger. The strings seem as agitated as the snow, the percussion as frozen as the sleet, the electronics as charged as the air. Sound bends around the cymbals like sheets of ice. In the sixth minute, a sound like clomping hooves comes across like a phantasm. The actual storm mixes with the impression of the storm to convey feelings of being trapped inside or wandering outside: stir crazy or snow-blind. The applause at the very end is well-earned. We’re not sure how many more Antarctic recordings Samartzis has in the bag, but as so few of us are likely to hear them in person, each release arrives as a revelation. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: experimental / field recording / ambient drone / electroacoustic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以2016年Casey研究站36小时暴风雪为素材基础，将极端环境中的风声、金属碰撞、无线电杂讯等田野录音与电子音效、弦乐、打击乐融合。Samartzis负责电子部分，Vorfeld提供弦乐器与人声化的金属声效，两者共同构建出一场关于极地科考环境的声景叙事。专辑从缓慢增强的风声与白噪声展开，逐步过渡到纯粹的打击乐段落，呈现暴风雪不同阶段的声音质地：既有机械失灵的嗡鸣，也有类似最后挣扎的零碎敲击。乐评强调录音素材本身的稀缺性与不可复制性，认为这类极地声学体验对于绝大多数听众而言只能通过此类作品间接获得。整体呈现出介于声音艺术、田野录音与实验音乐之间的跨域特质。

items.body: Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges Noxi Melank by ignatius   One of our favorite crafters of modular abstraction, glitch, and electronic noise, Ignatius (Buried In Time) makes a striking debut with Noxi Melank for Evel. Across eight pieces, sound worlds are explored, eroded, fragmented, and reshaped from start to finish. A surreal, broken rhythmic transition opens the nearly 10-minute opus “IdleDeep,” where blips, bleeps, echoes, scattered voices, and subdued electronic residue flicker beneath a slippery surface of decay. “GenderLimo” picks up the pace, remaining subtle, melankolic, and abstract as drifting, crumpled tones and drones take shape. Its sounds feel almost timeless, like abandoned and dented machines searching for somewhere to restart, mutate, and build unfamiliar worlds. As Ignatius’ glitch language unfolds piece by piece, each movement is marked by an unusually astute clarity within the noise. “Editorial,” for instance, reveals itself through Autechre meets Syl Kougaï-infused rhythmic deformation and energy, where modular structures seem to buckle, reconfigure, and find new momentum. While low-end rattling soundscapes provide a constant benchmark for Noxi Melank, Ignatius finds particular comfort in unusual time signatures—blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges, yet always moving forward with the precision of a practiced sound sculptor. Translucent structures of decay and erosion :: As the album persists, its tracks remain connected through an elusive, surreal logic. “Nonsequitirs” and “Locations” are especially revealing, unfolding as downtempo, almost translucent electroacoustic structures of decay and erosion. Dark passages maneuver through electronic debris, allowing fragments of rhythm and texture to surface before disappearing again. Closing with “SloxiEnds,” Ignatius shifts toward a more upbeat final chapter. Its Tri Repetae-like abstraction carries an unexpected sense of beauty, gradually transforming through layers of modular distortion—something the cover art depicts with uncanny precision—before arriving at an almost Eastern-sounding flourish. Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Noxi Melank is available on Evel. [Bandcamp] Noxi Melank by ignatiusThe post Ignatius :: Noxi Melank (Evel) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: Ignatius 在这张首作中让模块化系统持续失稳、重组，而非最终归位。八首曲目以电子噪声、故障节奏、低频轰鸣与稀疏采样构成不断变形的声景：开篇近十分钟的《IdleDeep》呈现模糊而幽暗的残响氛围；后续作品在Autechre式的节奏畸变与抽象段落之间切换，异常拍号在粗粝表面下保持清晰的结构感。末曲转向较为明亮、悦动的终章，并融入近似东方音色的收束，使整张专辑在腐朽、侵蚀与短暂的美感之间维持张力。独立发行，实验取向鲜明。

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There has been a big amount of albums that came before the King Crimson debut album "In court of the crimson king", that helped the shaping of the genre we call progressive rock. But it was this album that made waves and set the standards for progressive rock music for the years to come. The first album that it wasn't bluesy at all, but instead it was heavy and dark. The opening track "21st century schizoid man" sounds exactly like what you would expect to hear by only looking the album cover. Someone could say it sounds almost like Heavy Metal. The frantic last part of the song leads to the next song "I talk to the wind", an ethereal prayer, where the band shows its' softer side. The first side of the record, closes with the timeless epic classic "Epitaph'. Simply one of the best songs ever written, generally in music. "Moonchild" opens the second side of the record and it's a spellbinding tune, with majestic sounds from Ian McDonald. The haunting last part of the song, with the distant sounds, it's the perfect prologue for the closing track of the album, "The court of the crimson king", a medieval-like epic. "In the court of the crimson king" is a cornerstone of progressive rock, and if you ask me, King Crimson never matched it. Glorious.

items._cn_summary: 1969年的皇后的宫廷以强烈的不规则结构、密集的器乐铺陈和阴郁沉重的氛围，重新定义了前卫摇滚。开场曲以近乎失序的急促段落制造压迫感，副歌旋律却简洁有力，被作者形容为已有重金属气质；随后转入空灵祷词般的抒情篇章。第一面以经典长曲收束，第二面则由迷幻旋律、 Ian McDonald 的萨克斯独奏以及渐远的声场衔接至收尾。评论认为该专辑不仅超越了此前偏布鲁斯的前卫作品，更为后来确立兼具文学性、实验性与力度美学的标准。

items.body: The latest installment in the Portraits GRM series pairs the duo of crys cole & Oren Ambarchi with Italian maestro Giuseppe Ielasi. Each occupying a full side of vinyl, the result is a document of where contemporary sound practice finds itself in 2026 while paying homage to the institutional framework that made such work possible. This is not musique concrète in the traditional sense, but it is undeniably born from the same spirit of inquiry that drove Pierre Schaeffer to upend our relationship with sound nearly eighty years ago. Pierre Schaeffer (1910-1995) is remembered not necessarily for his music, or even his philosophical contributions to the study of sound (which were significant), but for his institution building. After pioneering musique concrète while working in French radio in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Schaeffer began almost instantly institutionalizing his legacy, what became the Groupe de Recherches Musicales (GRM) in 1958 (known as Ina-GRM since 1975). The tension between preserving a tradition and remaining open to the new has defined the institution ever since. My 2019 interview with François J. Bonnet—composer, philosopher, and current director of Ina-GRM—explored precisely this question: how does an institution honor its past while making space for the unfamiliar? An answer arrived in 2020 with the launch of Portraits GRM, a series of commissioned releases designed to bring contemporary voices into the GRM’s hallowed studios. The first release was Jim O’Rourke’s Shutting Down Here, fittingly so, as his sessions there spanned 30 years and thus that work’s completion constituted the closing of a significant loop. The re-issuing of classic and adjacent GRM titles began under the direction of Editions Mego, but after the death of Peter Rehberg (Pita) in 2021, the series transitioned to the stewardship of Shelter Press. Since then, Portraits GRM has featured Lucy Railton, Okkyung Lee, Kali Malone, Lasse Marhaug, Laurel Halo, Beatrice Dillon, and many others—artists who share little aesthetically but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do. As with most installments in the series, the latest release offers two compelling sidelong works from heavyweights of the experimental underground. On one side, crys cole and Oren Ambarchi continue their collaborative exploration of texture and density; on the other, Giuseppe Ielasi presents something distinctly his own. crys cole & Oren Ambarchi ~ Sparkling or Silent The title suggests something binary—a flickering between presence and absence, articulation and withholding—but the piece itself operates in the spaces between. Sparkling or Silent opens with what might best be described as ASMR-concrète: close-mic’d rustling, breath, the micro-articulations of objects manipulated in near-silence. It is intimate yet abstract, as though the listener has stumbled upon a private ritual. Over its 19’43’’ duration, the work unfolds in several distinct movements, each building upon the last until the accumulated density becomes something else entirely. Oren Ambarchi needs little introduction. The Australian guitarist has built a formidable reputation as a solo artist and one of the most prolific collaborators in experimental music, with a discography that touches on everything from the glacial drone of his solo work to the rhythmic propulsion of his trio with Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin—whose Ghosted series has only grown more assured with each installment. Records including Grapes from the estate (2004), Hubris (2016), and Simian Angel (2019) are personal favorites, not to mention his ongoing dialogues with figures like Keiji Haino and Jim O’Rourke. But alongside this celebrated career, there exists another body of work, equally significant if less discussed: his partnership with crys cole. Likely the less familiar name to many listeners, cole’s work is no less deserving of attention. I have been a fan of this Canadian sound artist’s practice for years, both in her solo work and her collaborations. Her third album for Black Truffle, Making Conversation collects three recent commissioned pieces and demonstrates a trajectory that has moved steadily toward greater formal control without sacrificing the tactile, almost sculptural quality of her sound. She had been involved with Winnipeg’s send + receive festival for over a decade, contributed photographs and projections to classic Canadian experimental records, and continues to be an active performer and sound artist. Her work with Ora Clementi—the duo with James Rushford—offers a dense thicket of sonic material that feels both organic and constructed. Sylva Sylvarum, in particular, stands as a high-water mark in her collaborative output. On Ambarchi’s Audience of One (2012), she’s credited as contributing contact microphones and brushes to the track “Passage.” They’ve since produced several records as a duo: Sonja Henies Vei 31 (2014), a hazy collage of intimate gesture and field recordings from a Norwegian sojourn; Hotel Record (2017), its title a dryly witty reference to its origins in hotel room sessions, a study in digital textures; and Gallivant (2021), documenting a live concert from the previous year. The pair have often played with others, including Keith Rowe and Leif Elggren. The collaborative dynamic is worth dwelling on, if only because there is something peculiar and generative about a musical duo that is also a romantic couple. One thinks of the historical precedents: Sonny and Linda Sharrock, whose volatile partnership produced some of the most ferocious free jazz of the late 1960s and early 1970s; Max Roach and Abby Lincoln, whose work together addressed civil rights with a moral urgency that still resonates, again overshadowed by a documented history of abuse. More recently, and hopefully less problematically, I think of Christina Vantzou and John Also Bennett, Matmos (MC Schmidt and Drew Daniel), and Two-Way Street—Ashlee Booth on cello and Adam Lion on percussion, for whom Sarah Hennies wrote a piece exploring precicely the dynamic between a romantic and musical partnership. Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe have even released a few short pieces as Eselsohr. There is something about the intimacy of shared life that translates into the shared space of improvisation and composition, a trust that allows for risk without the safety net of distance. A residency abroad, a portrait of two artists developing a shared vocabulary in confined spaces, the energy of a live recording. Sparkling or Silent represents something different—a consciously composed concert work. As the Portraits GRM materials describe it, the piece is “a moment apart in their respective artistic approaches” where an electroacoustic method that has always been latent in both of their practices “here asserts itself as a central compositional modality.” This shift from documentation to composition makes Sparkling or Silent feel more expansive and considered, even if it doesn’t necessarily represent a linear “evolution” so much as a deliberate side-step into a different mode of working. From its intimate opening, Sparkling or Silent gradually accumulates tonal densisty before dissolving again. About halfway through, after cohering into a sustained drone cloud, the texture thins; ghostly melodies and gentle rustlings emerge from the haze, while field recordings slowly ground us in an unexpected place. The real surprise arrives in the final four minutes: a sudden chorus of truck (?) horn harmonies. The effect recalls Alvin Curran’s Maritime Rites, transposed from water to asphalt; the collective ritual of Curran’s foghorns replaced by the found sounds of the highway. Within a minute, these sounds accumulate into a dense, surprisingly consonant cluster, overlapping blares forming a sustained fog of noise that continues until, finally, the sparkle turns to silence. It is a closing gesture that reframes everything that came before, revealing the delicate rustlings of the opening as part of a larger soundscape that extends far beyond the studio walls. The piece does not so much end as disperse, its constituent parts returning to the world from which they were borrowed.   Giuseppe Ielasi ~ unfamiliar music (paris) In Milano in 2017, I met Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe for dinner accompanied by Oren and crys, who were part-time residents of the city then—their European headquarters, before relocating to Berlin, was this underrated Italian metropolis, a base between their Australian and Canadian homelands. So in my mind, the connection between the artists featured on this record is obvious, forged not only through shared aesthetics but through shared meals, shared cities, shared lives. But Ielasi’s relationship to this series extends far beyond personal connections. He has mastered every Portraits GRM record except the first, and his own Senufo label released early records by Kassel Jaeger, which was in fact my introduction to François J. Bonnet many years ago. This record, then, feels like a culmination; the current director of Ina-GRM, the mastering engineer, the series, and the artists all intertwined in a web of mutual influence and respect that spans decades. Ielasi’s catalog is deep and varied, marked by a restless curiosity that refuses to settle into comfortable routines. He has his interests and proclivities—a fascination with small sounds, repetition, motors, unusual rhythmic grooves, in other words “an insistence on material”—but he rarely deploys the same technical setup or approach twice, constantly searching for new means of expression. This commitment to renewal is evident throughout his discography, from his early work on the 12k label to his more recent return to explorations of guitar and electronics. unfamiliar music (paris) arrives with some precedent. Ielasi has performed at the GRM before; I have a recording from 20 January 2014 at GRM Paris that captures his take on acousmatic diffusion. The title itself is shared with unfamiliar music vol.1 (guitar duets), a 2024 digital record that expanded a renewed focus on guitar as a sound source that began with releases in 2020. But what connection does this new piece have to that earlier work? The title seems to refer less to a specific genre or instrumentation and more to a mode of production, an approach to working with sound that prioritizes the strange, the dislocated, the not-quite-familiar. The cover of this release depicts Ielasi performing in Paris with a sampler, suggesting a process rooted in improvisation and constraint. And indeed, some of the samples in the piece do seem to be shared with previously released works, here recontextualized and repurposed. This is not a work of pure creation ex nihilo but of rearrangement, of finding new relationships between existing materials, a practice that echoes both the concrète tradition as well as Ielasi’s own history of pushing it into new territory. The GRM’s acousmatic tradition is evident in the microphone technique and in the spatial treatment of sounds, but there is also a digital air to the proceedings that feels distinctly contemporary, a reminder that the techniques Schaeffer pioneered have been absorbed, transformed, and rendered nearly invisible in the work of subsequent generations. Where cole and Ambarchi’s contribution moves from intimacy to surreal mundanity, Ielasi’s work operates in a different register entirely. The piece itself unfolds as a study in gentle contrast and rhythmic accumulation. The rhythmic elements that have long characterized his work are present but transformed—pulses that never quite lock into a predictable groove, small sounds that build into larger textures, a sense of propulsion that constantly threatens to derail itself. Static gives way to layers of competing rhythm gives way to a mobile lullaby. unfamiliar music (paris) passes through a range of sonic territories without any clear delineations between movements. Ielasi opts instead for a gradual process of substitution. What emerges is a piece that feels both of its moment and somehow outside of it. The “unfamiliar” of the title is not a description of the sounds themselves but of the relationships between them, the way they refuse to settle into expected patterns or resolve into comfortable listening. Ielasi makes music that demands attention without demanding understanding, that rewards close listening without promising easy rewards.   Taken together with the cole and Ambarchi piece, this release offers a portrait of the series at its best: two works that share little in common but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do, and a commitment to the kind of exploration that Schaeffer himself would have recognized. The Portraits GRM series continues to honor its institutional legacy not through preservation but through renewal, not by looking backward but by making space for the unfamiliar. (Joseph Sannicandro)

items._cn_summary: Portraits GRM系列最新一期由crys cole与Oren Ambarchi合作、Giuseppe Ielasi各自呈现长篇作品，向法国具象音乐研究机构GRM致敬。评论追溯了GRM自Pierre Schaeffer以来的机构建设历程，以及该系列自2020年启动以来在Editions Mego（Peter Rehberg去世后）转由Shelter Press发行的脉络。crys cole与Ambarchi的作品以近距拾音的细碎声响开场，在寂静中挖掘物体的微观动态，19分多钟的篇幅在质感与密度的渐变中展开，介于在场与缺席、显形与隐匿之间的张力贯穿始终。Ielasi侧则延续其个人风格，与前者形成对照。整张专辑是当代声响实践在GRM录音棚传统中的一次承续与对话，延续了该系列对实验音乐边界的持续推进。

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. Intro (Mafar) featuring local vocals, a melancholic guitar sound worthy of Anathema, a melody reminiscent of the *The Persuaders!* theme, and stereo keyboards undulating between the speakers. Elegance, abstract Oriental rock, traditional instruments?in short, a perfect soundscape evoking life in a land that symbolizes religious massacres.2. "Nsina El 'Inwan" follows?a sad, intimate ballad driven by piano and a resigned-sounding guitar; Jeries' vocals demonstrate how a voice, when well-integrated into a tune, enhances the track without stifling the melody.3. "Min El Nar Khayfen" features crystalline keyboard work answering a sparkling guitar, with a touch of vintage organ. Philippe launches a killer guitar solo?a moment suggesting that peace is actually possible.4. "Esma' O Shouf" shifts into new-wave/darkwave mode; the rhythm guitar starts with a 60s "gangster" vibe before drifting into an 80s Marillion style, then moving toward the new-millennium sound of Riverside?fabulous. And let's not forget Raji's organ, which melts the heart; in short, it's great to rediscover them and dive back into their music.5. "Fatah 'Eneih" follows, built on a plaintive organ and guitar interplay. It has a sluggish start, then builds into a crescendo of incredible tension that wanders off into dreamlike prog, flirting with black/heavy/prog metal. Marwan's bass rides a Pink Floyd wave before washing up against a jazzy piano; the prog sound drifts along with an austere heavy riff and a haunting, persistent keyboard line. Never a dull moment.6. "Ana Malet" features a groovy, grunge-tinged riff and vocals worthy of the Sex Pistols?throwing caution to the wind: where are they headed? In any case, it's delightful to see this fusion of styles. Just as I'm settling in, the thunderous 80s-style sax from Jeries pulls us back into mainstream rock. A touch of melancholic guitar?reminiscent of Anathema?and I'm hooked.7. "El Leil Bhal 'Oyoun" returns to the Mafar sound?a welcome shift. It's a bouncy alternative track, driven by distant, heavy guitar notes. A flirtation between metal and dark rock, with the sax magically tying it all together. A track that shines thanks to its build-up and that melancholic guitar?it's a real thrill for me?leading into a soaring finale that veers into metal for that massive sound.8. "Sada" follows, pulling the same trick: a restrained, metallic guitar riff punching through against a backdrop of ethereal piano. The Anathema vibe keeps coming back to me; the piano outro, gently picking out its final notes, is simply admirable.9. The true "Outro" arrives, blending synth, violin, and melancholic guitar, all bolstered by a rich, melting organ?pure listening pleasure.An album to help you live?almost as if nothing were wrong?in this dehumanized territory; a little music to help you survive.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自中东地区，是一张跨界前卫摇滚作品，将东方传统音乐元素与西方前卫摇滚语汇相融合。评论提及多首曲目展现出复杂的器乐编排：键盘与钢琴构建氛围基底，吉他独奏兼具忧郁与爆发力，萨克斯的穿插为作品注入意外色彩。整体风格在Crossover Prog的框架内融合了暗潮律动、新浪潮节奏乃至金属元素，同时保留了中东传统乐器的音色特征。评论反复将其与Anathema、Marillion、Riverside等乐队相比，表明作品具有较强的欧洲前卫摇滚血统。专辑名为阿拉伯语，暗示其承载着特定地域文化语境，试图以音乐形式回应该地区的现实处境。作为来自非主流音乐地区的独立厂牌发行作品，其跨文化融合视角和地域特色使其具有独特的艺术价值。

items.body: Review by meurdhek — Nearly 50 years that we've been waiting for these recordings! They have finally reached us in the form of a CD packed to the brim.Here, then, is Xalph, with its creative and warm take on Zeuhl, embracing us and happily plunging us back into the excitement of those years at the end of Magma's first incarnation, when excellent bands emerged from its orbit and carved their own paths through the lava of the world Magma had created.Besides shedding some Soleil Zeuhl light on these recordings, this edition finally sets the record straight, putting things back in order and into perspective, after the Monster M�lodies edition made two mistakes when the LP was released in 2018.The first stated: "This record contains the track 'Gya-Tei' in its entirety, a track of which only part had previously appeared on the Enneade compilation of new music, released in 1987."Yet this track had in fact already been released in its entirety on the Enneade compilation...The second claim was made with no small amount of audacity, or perhaps simply out of ignorance: "This record contains all of this legendary group's studio recordings."We now know that this was false. In fact, all the recordings on this CD had already been circulating online for decades under the title "Demos 1975-1980", albeit in inferior-sounding versions.One could even argue that the best tracks were not chosen for the Monster M�lodies LP. "Xessanderelph", "Exorde" and "Ter" keep you on the edge of your seat, and while some of the other tracks may initially seem softer, with occasional lulls, every track contains passages and endings of epic, exultant, even blazing progressive Zeuhl. This is further reinforced by the addition of vocals, which undoubtedly immerse Xalph even more deeply in the genre's established conventions, shaped by the model that bears Vander's signature, while pushing the jazz-rock aspect of their music slightly further into the background.With the exception of Gya-Tei, all the tracks presented here had therefore remained unreleased in this particular form. Nevertheless, we find the intro to "Entr�e d'Am�lie" and "Ballade � Xalph" on the LP in earlier versions that one might even prefer. The addition of soprano saxophone undoubtedly gives them a more soaring lyrical quality, while the later versions recorded at Studio Isis bring a more pronounced sense of tension, with the guitar pushed further to the forefront.In any case, if I were to indulge in a shortcut, I would say that Xessander's presents countless moments of musical grace and daring, drawn from the finest vintage of Zeuhl jazz-rock lava. It would have been a shame if we had never had the chance to enjoy them.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了法国Zeuhl乐队Xalph在1975至1980年间制作的录音，由小厂牌Zeuhl于2026年重新整理发行。乐评重点纠正了此前Monster Mélodies LP版本的两个错误说法——该合辑并非首度收录'Gya-Tei'完整版，也不是乐队全部录音。评论指出'Demos 1975-1980'早已在网络上流传，但音质较差；此版精选了'Xessanderelph''Exorde''Ter'等最佳曲目，每首都包含壮丽激昂的Zeuhl段落。录音呈现了该流派典型的Vander式特征：人声的加入使作品更贴合类型惯例，吉他被推至更突出的位置，高音萨克斯的加入赋予某些早期版本更抒情的飞升感，而后期Studio Isis版本则强化了紧张感。整体展现了Zeuhl爵士摇滚最具创造力时期的音乐面貌。

items.body: Review by Logan — The history of Boc Maxima functions like a rogue transmission. Distributed as a private 1996 cassette to a small inner circle of family and friends, it eventually leaked into the early-2000s file-sharing ether and became a foundational internet myth. Rather than a mere collection of loose bedroom demos, the tape serves as the unredacted genetic blueprint for what Boards of Canada would become. Context alters the architecture. A sound wave does not change its geometry, but its impact shifts based on the reified bounds of the sequence. Sequenced between dark, lo-fi vignettes and deliberate, haunting fade-ins, these familiar melodies lose their polished studio insulation. The timeline functions less like a passive playlist and more like a continuous midnight broadcast.The movement of this tape carries the uncanny dimensions of The Twilight Zone, where science meets superstition, alongside the OBLIVION signal in Cronenberg's Videodrome, and the unrepeatable frequency of the 1977 Wow! signal. The bleeding transitions carry a distinct Blue Jam late-night radio logic. The sequencing introduces an invasive quality that alters how the listening space decodes this familiar pastoral nostalgia, inducing a state of quiet suspension where childhood memory and cold, apocalyptic dread exist in an uneasy harmony. Long live the new flesh.
items._cn_summary: 这张1996年的私密卡带录音被视为Boards of Canada日后成熟作品的原始基因图谱。评论聚焦于专辑独特的聆听语境与序列编排：曲目之间通过黑暗、低保真的声景片段和刻意的渐入渐出相互连接，营造出深夜广播般的连续传输感。乐评将其与《阴阳魔界》的诡异维度、Videodrome的失控信号以及1977年Wow!信号的不可重复频率相类比，强调作品营造的不安氛围——田园式怀旧记忆与末世冷酷恐惧共存于一种悬停的听觉状态中。评论指出，脱离正式录音棚润色后，这些熟悉旋律展现出粗糙原始的质感，序列结构本身成为侵入性元素，重新编码了听者对声音空间的感知。整体呈现出一种介于童年温暖与超自然恐惧之间的病理地带美学。

items.body: Label: ECM Records, 2026 Personnel - Enrico Rava: trumpet; Joe Lovano: tenor saxophone, tarogato; Matteo Paggi: trombone; Francesco Diodati: guitar; Francesco Ponticelli: bass; Evita Pollidoro: drums, vocals. Illustrious Italian trumpeter and composer Enrico Rava, a longtime force on the European jazz scene, returns with his Fearless Five ensemble, welcoming guest saxophonist Joe Lovano, a powerhouse improviser who had collaborated with the bandleader on the live recording Roma (ECM, 2019). All members of the quintet contribute compositions, trusting the bandleader's candidly investigative approach that opposes rigid perceptions. Rava's " Certi Angoli Segreti ", an exceptionally beautiful tune first recorded in 1998, gracefully materializes with beautiful color shades. Francesco Diodati's guitar gives it a particular touch, later soloing with motivic ability and acerbic distortion; Francesco Ponticelli's dynamic bass builds a solid foundation with drummer Evita Polidoro; Lovano's storytelling comes with delightful details; trombonist Matteo Paggi's expressions are grounded and exploratory; and Rava excels in his improvisational fluctuations—sometimes angular and outside, other times hypnotically flowing and distinctively melodic. Rava brings two other previously recorded pieces: " Hitchcock at the Beach ", whose balladic feeling and original beauty are preserved despite emerging here most as a collaborative voice-trumpet meditation; and the exciting " Bowery Dance ", which evokes Rava's New York years with an electrified intro, authoritative bass double-stops, and a crisp backbeat. Lovano and Rava improvise with fire, rejoicing in unison lines in support of their declarations. Lovano is credited with a couple of distinct compositions. The open-ended " Sun Rava " is full of possibilities, incorporating sharp staccato blows, buoyant swing impulses, and clever pedal points, also featuring improvised dialogues between Rava and Paggi, and then Diodati and Lovano, before the saxophonist rambles freely over the bass-and-drums bedrock. " Tone, Shape, and Colours ", a free improvisation based on a riff by Lovano, brings the horn players together in lively conversation. If the rhythm section kicks into high gear on Lovano's pieces, it eases into the softer lyrical flow of Diodati's " Sin Peso ", a burnished ballad suggesting a bolero feel, and Polidoro's " Le Mie Gambe ", which, unfolding in 3/4, features the drummer as a vocalist of surprising intensity. Since the early '70s, Rava—who turned 87 in August—has led a series of highly rewarding albums, and Corners is no exception. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Certi Angoli Segreti ► 06 - Tune, Shape, and Colours ► 08 - Bowery Dance

items._cn_summary: 意大利小号手恩里科·拉瓦与恐惧五人组迎来萨克斯手乔·洛瓦诺回归，共同完成这张自由即兴与现代作曲并重的唱片。全员参与创作，曲目涵盖早年旧作与新曲，既有柔软抒情叙事，也有尖锐断奏、摇摆脉冲和开放式对话。洛瓦诺的曲目充分解放节奏组，拉瓦则在棱角分明的即兴与催眠般流动的旋律间切换。吉他、长号、贝斯和鼓各具鲜明声音，尤其后者兼任人声，在三拍子的《我的双腿》中展现意外张力。ECM的录音保持了清晰质感与空间感，使这张作品兼具结构控制和探索性。

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — The progressive metal movement, whose foundations were first laid in the mid-to-late 1980s by pioneers such as Queensr�che, Fates Warning, and Dream Theater, gained a much stronger identity and momentum during the 1990s, eventually expanding and establishing itself as a fully-fledged genre in the 2000s. Redemption belongs to the group of bands that emerged under that inspiring influence, shaping a powerful and virtuosic musical approach, immersed in the intricate structures of the most contemporary prog metal.With their self-titled 2003 debut album, Redemption had already shown what they were capable of, although it was still a somewhat raw and unpolished power-metal-style offering with nascent progressive elements. For "The Fullness of Time" (2005), their second album, the band led by Nick van Dyk brought in the duo James Sherwood (bass) and Chris Quirarte (drums), both from the ranks of the Los Angeles-based band Prymary, as their new rhythm section, and, most importantly, vocalist Ray Alder -who also fronted Fates Warning- evolving toward a more defined and mature sound.The first third of the album retains the band's seminal sound, with machine-gun-like, galloping riffs; frenzied, counterpointing solos between Bernie Versailles and van Dyk; and Quirarte's wild double-bass drumming, to which van Dyk's keyboards add an additional, fitting melodic and atmospheric layer, both on the aggressive "Threads," the fast-paced "Scarred," and the reflective and bitter "Parker's Eyes" -which offers a somber and disheartening view of the world, including a reference to the events of 9/11- and incorporates a beautiful, arpeggiated acoustic nuance before exploding instrumentally.The following two-thirds reflect the band's solidity and progressive character, with the epic "Sapphire", a powerful and expansive instrumental tapestry led by a spirited Alder on vocals and generous with guitar and synthesizer solos, contrasted with calm, refreshing passages -the jewel of the album- and the intricate "The Fullness of Time," a suite divided into four sections where journeys through rocky peaks -the furious and vengeful "i. Rage" and the resilient "iii. Release"- alternate with clear, evocative sonic valleys -the meditative "ii. Despair" and the hopeful and luminous "iv. Trascendence"."The Fullness of Time" marked a turning point in Redemption's career: an album in which the band left behind the rough edges of its debut to find its own identity, delivering one of the genre's strongest offerings of the mid-2000s.4/4.5 stars
items._genre: progressive metal / progressive rock / power metal
items._cn_summary: 这是Redemption继同名首作后的第二张专辑，也是乐队风格成熟的转折点。新阵容加入贝斯手James Sherwood、鼓手Chris Quirarte与主唱Ray Alder，保留了高速连缀riff、双吉他对位独奏与键盘铺陈。前段作品延续锐利直接的冲击感，后段则展开更完整的结构探索：七分钟器乐巨作Sapphire与四乐章同名组曲，以激烈段落和沉静段落交替推进，呈现从愤怒、绝望到释放、超脱的起伏。整体摆脱首作的粗糙感，在技术展示、动态控制和旋律层次上均达到较高完成度。

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Released in 2007 through the bands official fan club, 'Images and Words 15th Anniversary Performance' is literally what it says it is; Dream Theater playing the entire album that forever set the standard for all progressive metal bands to follow. Of course, it has its pros and cons. There's some interesting embellishments dotted around, which could keep us prog nerds at least somewhat invested for a little while, and it's cool to hear Jordan Rudess interpret some of Kevin Moore's keyboard parts. Then of course, there's vocalist James LaBrie. Sure, he struggles with some of it due to age and a well-documented vocal injury, but I guess at least he's trying. The band would go on to release a 25th anniversary performance of this album through their 'Lost Not Forgotten' series many years later, so, you know, it's probably slightly better than that one, again, due to LaBrie being another ten years older by then and struggling even more. Bless him. I don't think I'd ever choose to actually listen to this over the original 1992 studio album, which, for the record, is my favourite album of all time. But the name of this release describes exactly what you're getting here, so there's absolutely no point in taking it too seriously. It's a cool addition to the collection, and if you're a die-hard Dream Theater fan like I am, then you'll enjoy owning it. Simple as that.

items.body: Review by Logan — Returning to Hi Scores after spending time with the heavy, dark sound of Inferno is like finding an old, clean blueprint before it weathered. This 1996 EP finds the Sandison brothers at a time when their geometric tracking methods were sharp and exposed, before their focus shifted toward deep analogue erosion. It occupies a distinct place in their discography, bypassing the fragile sentimentality of their later records. The sound functions as a raw, intense environment rather than electronic escapism, following an internal logic that aligns with how my own mind navigates structure.The title track, "Hi Scores", relies on a clinical drive. Spending time with their wider catalogue highlights the unconventional nature of this upfront electro-funk grid. Originally released on Manchester's experimental Skam label, it establishes a stark, unpolished baseline belonging to the sharp mathematical grids of the mid-nineties IDM scene rather than a childhood memory. It reveals a naked skeletal frame, showing basic programming choices before the arrangements were buried in rich, atmospheric grime."Turquoise Hexagon Sun" is positioned next. Observing how this piece functions later on Music Has the Right to Children makes its placement here notable. It introduces the loop-based geometry and hexagonal motifs they would reference for decades. Yet, for all its melodic layers, it holds an unsettling tension. It is a track I turn off when the kids are around, since the underlying textures feel less like a comforting memory and more like a displaced, menacing transmission.The transition into "Nlogax" requires a distinct mental shift. Instead of a soft fade, the drop is sharp and jarring. The track triggers a physical response. The microtonal dissonance and aggressive, detuned synth hook warp the stereo field, producing a genuine sensation of vertigo and physical nausea."June 9th" follows this pitch instability, bringing a state of sensory hyper-vigilance. By layering skittering, fast percussion elements over a lagging breakbeat and burying muffled melodies under a low-end thrum, the duo compresses the perception of space, creating a claustrophobic acoustic environment. The complex, cinematic logic shares an architectural layout with The Future Sound of London's 1994 release, Lifeforms. Both share an uncompromising, alien framework that rejects simple dancefloor trends. On a surface listen, Hi Scores can seem disjointed, but immersion in this middle section shows how the segments serve a rigid purpose.The intensity of these tracks relates directly to the literal mechanical wow and flutter effect running through the tape machines. The severe pitch warps build an environment that feels suffocating, forcing a physical confrontation across the enteric nervous system."Seeya Later" works on an interesting psychological plane. Having tracked its connection back to Twoism, the track utilises heavy, drifting synth pads to tie the upfront grooves to the end of the record, drawing the brain down into a heavy twilight trance.The final track, "Everything You Do Is a Balloon", serves as a clear blueprint for their subsequent discography. In this non-sentimental context, however, the track offers little safe haven or comforting relief. It feels off-kilter, trading easy nostalgia for a heavy, visceral sonic power. Starting with a fragile, melancholic synth melody before dropping into a slow-motion hip-hop breakbeat, it functions less as a comforting exit and more as a substantial climax that carries the electro-acoustic DNA that would later anchor the dense harmonic textures of The Campfire Headphase.Over time, Hi Scores has realised its full potential as a five-star record for me. It operates more like a raw template for psychological disruption than a standard piece of auditory expression. Spending time with all of their albums reinforces the essential nature of this blueprint, landing as an intense, disorienting, and highly effective release.
items._cn_summary: 这是Boards of Canada 1996年发行于曼彻斯特Skam实验厂牌的EP，被视为其后续作品的原始骨架。评论者将这张EP置于乐队完整作品谱系中审视，指出此时期Sandison兄弟的几何式编曲方法尚未被后来的模拟氛围层叠所遮蔽，呈现出裸露的编程逻辑与锐利的电子放克网格。标题曲强调临床式的机械律动，'Turquoise Hexagon Sun'呈现不安的旋律张力，'Nlogax'通过微分音失谐与立体声场扭曲引发眩晕般的生理反应，'June 9th'以跳切的打击层与滞后碎拍压缩空间感知，构建密闭的声学环境。磁带机的抖晃失真贯穿整体，迫使听者与肠道神经系统产生直接的身体对抗。整体中段各曲构成严密的逻辑链，排斥简单的舞池取向。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is no coincidence that many electronic music artists draw inspiration from the past, specifically the 1970s. The British duo Boards of Canada creates a sound that feels progressive in an electronic sense, much like the Norwegian duo R�yksopp has done at times. It is the art of layering sounds, not haphazardly, but with a very clear purpose: to evoke moods and suggest mental images or ideas that often transcend mere musical concepts. The cover of their debut album, Music Has the Right to Children, always struck me as very retro, very 1960s, yet upon closer inspection, much like a painting bearing an artist's signature, one discovers that the figures lack actual faces. They are blank slates, leaving the viewer to imagine what lies within. "An Eagle in Your Mind" offers a magnetic groove, featuring a downtempo rhythm with a strong, minimalist trip-hop foundation. The track combines an organic drum feel with the presence of both samples and scratching, making it highly appealing and modern; it also reminds me of another underground classic, Vernon Reid's first solo album, Mistaken Identity (1996), which blended heavy guitar work with electronic elements and featured DJ Logic.Short tracks like "The Color of the Fire" reminded me, in the spaces between the longer pieces, of the intros on Gong's Angel's Egg, as well as the poetic ambient atmospheres of Brian Eno. The use of analog synthesizers also draws a parallel to another electronic duo, the French group Air, and in "Telephasic Workshop," we can observe how two parallel paths, traced by Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin respectively, overlap: one line is a steady, unwavering, and steadfast drone, while the other plays solos and varies, confident in the support of its stable counterpart."Sixtyten" is spacey and psychedelic, yet syncopated; the ghostly voices lending mystery to the final mix appear like palace spies straight out of Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights. I find funk and jazz elements in Turquoise Hexagon Sun; ambient music can be that rich, Brian Eno knows a lot about that, too, and his spirit is present on this album as well. It's about not being afraid to experiment and treating music like water: if it spills, it doesn't disappear, it simply changes shape.The bridges turn into short songs in their own right, tracks with their own distinct identity, such as "Kaini Industries" or "Bocuma", a synthesizer part that can evoke a natural waterfall, or statues coming to life at night... and "Roygbiv," which fuses a hip-hop beat with a highly symphonic, atmospheric mood, yet possesses just the right touch to feel fresh, almost New Wave, thanks to a simple keyboard, like those three-prong outlets. "Rue The Whirl" represents the brand of progressive electronica that appeals to me most; its tension builds steadily, an electronic record charged with alternating current. Through waves of sound, it achieves a passive, psychedelic atmosphere, almost a trance state, yet one not devoid of variation, as it ultimately flirts with dissonance and details like Mellotrons, striking the perfect balance between the vintage and the postmodern.The secret behind the change in sound, so percussive and featuring a sort of equidistant echo, in "Aquarius" is a slap-funk sample from the song of the same name from the movie Hair (1979). The narrative voice, the children's laughter, reminiscent of what Rickie Lee Jones used on her album Pop Pop, and those percussive variations combined to create a hybrid that was also hypnotic. Pete Standing Alone returns to those minimalist Brian Eno-esque melodies, but incorporates samples that introduce variations and shifts in rhythm, preventing the listener from settling into a routine, as the aim is to keep the sonic progression moving forward."Smokes Quantity" is rhythm with substance, a melody that provokes and leaves a lasting mark, keeping the mind wide awake; Boards of Canada offers an inward journey that challenges one's comfort zone, much like atonal music once did. Only then are we ready for "Open the Light," with its emotive, Vangelis-esque progression, for it is wrong to skip chapters that were sequenced in a specific order to prime the mood and ensure receptiveness to the climax of the penultimate track, experiencing it for what it truly is: a sonic journey.
items._cn_summary: 这张1998年的电子专辑以层层叠加的声音构建为核心技法，通过模拟合成器、采样与打碟等手段塑造出极具画面感的心理氛围。评论者将其与Röyksopp、Air等电子组合及Brian Eno的氛围音乐精神相联系，指出短小曲目如过渡桥段般串联起整体结构。长曲如Rue The Whirl以渐进式张力构建迷幻电流感，而Turquoise Hexagon Sun与Roygbiv则融合放克、爵士与嘻哈节拍，在简洁键盘音色与交响化氛围之间取得平衡。整体制作强调声音的有机性与实验精神，模拟合成器营造出70年代怀旧质感的同时保持现代感，是电子音乐领域中兼具艺术深度与可听性的里程碑式作品。

items.body: Syndey Valette I Fucking Love You Artoffact Records I Fucking Love You represents a pretty big swing for Paris’ Sydney Valette. Where his material has always leaned into the history of dignified continental darkwave, Valette has never been afraid to inject some urgency, emotion and a dollop of dry humor into the proceedings. For this record he’s kicked those instincts into overdrive, making the most lively and varied album of his career to date. It’s a tightrope to maintain his measured approach to composition and performance while also letting those qualities that have previously been around the edges take a more direct spotlight, and Valette walks it with confidence and skill. Part of the record’s personality comes from how lively and ready to go the songs sound; not minimal by any means, but not overly ornamented or overworked. Opener “Warrior” is made up of a chirpy synth lead that has an almost futurepop sound, paired with a simple kick-clap drum pattern to drive it, his grave vocals, vocoder and samples from The Exorcist to fill it out. It’s effective because it’s simple and dramatic without seeming crass, a quality shared by such cuts as “Relèves-toi” whose mute pulsing bassline is punctuated by bursts of timpani and synthesized pipes, grand and even cinematic in scope, but not crowded or excessive. And when Valette really goes for the vocal gusto on the title track’s widescreen synthpop, dropping his often grave vocal delivery for a wounded croon and yelped and shouted backing, he keeps the speedy synths and drums behind him, giving himself the push and momentum for take-off. Whether those canny arrangement and delivery choices are instinctual or the product of hours of work, they really do make I Fucking Love You the album it is. Russian language cut “Как Свеча” certainly has the gravity inherent to the language as sung, and chooses to lay back in delivering its chorus, creating a tension between its melancholic and funereal mood and its zippy tempo. In perhaps the album’s most ambitious moment, closer “No Ibiza For Mr. Valette”, he goes with a plainer vocal style and uses some of his dry humor to play off what is clearly a song of heartbreak, the song slowly graduating from simple synths and drums to lush pads. Like the rest of the album, what makes it great is how it communicates so much emotionally and thematically without needing to state anything openly, saying very little but telling us everything. Buy it. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette The post Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是巴黎暗潮艺人迄今为止最具活力与变化的一次尝试。评论指出，Valette 长期扎根欧陆暗潮传统，但此次大胆注入紧迫感、情感张力与冷幽默，在克制作曲与放纵表达之间走钢丝。开篇曲以未来流行质感的明亮合成器主导，搭配《驱魔人》对白采样与人声 vocoder，制造出简洁却戏剧化的效果。法语曲目在合成器管风琴与定音鼓中铺陈出影院般的壮阔感，标题曲则让人声从一贯的低沉转为受伤式哭腔。俄语曲目利用语言本身的庄重感制造丧葬氛围与明快节奏之间的张力。终曲从简朴的合成器节奏逐渐过渡到丰满的铺垫层，在不直白表达的前提下完成情感的全面释放。整体编排既有节制又充满张力，每首歌都保持着流动的能量与适度装饰之间的平衡。

items.body: One of several promising artists emerging from a wave of new blood in the DMV-area scene, Will Graham’s adventurous solo project Vasterian is still in the process of defining his sound. His first tape Static Dreams employed heavy use of radio to conjure a sputtering soundscape full of dead air and hiss, a stark contrast to the inaugural live set I saw him play earlier this year that consisted of bracing, bellowing power electronics. Though his output thus far doesn’t display a consistent style (far from a bad thing, to be sure), there’s certainly a consistent level of intent and execution. Brand new C44 Turn Around plays like an attempt to flesh out the middle ground between the disparate extremes of the debut release and performance, and a successful attempt at that. Graham structures the two sides around texture shifts between the garbled warbles of intercepted transmissions and the screech of analog feedback, opting for a patient freeform progression with plenty of room to breathe. The A-spanning “On Plummer’s Island” [sic] blooms slowly and steadily, with wounded, barely legible speech giving way to oscillating static rent with high-frequency slice ‘n dice. When the track hits its peak it’s thrilling, so howling and unstable that it feels like the tape is going to burn right through your deck. The facing pair of the title cut and “Tracing the Spiral / Smooth Character” are more pensive. Both feel fragile and vulnerable in their raw simplicity, especially when Graham flips on the vocal mic at the end of the latter and lays down some agonized shouts over a seething mass of minor harmony, a more elegiac take on the cathartic aggression found in his work as Comfort & Critique. It’s a strong and haunting conclusion that offers a late anchor to the preceding potpourri and pays off the snatches of vocals heard throughout. Turn Around may have worked better as, say, a C30 (“On Plummer’s Island” especially starts to drag toward the end) and gets a bit bogged down by its own eclecticism, the abundance of creativity and passion make it memorable—and replayable. Copies are available from the label via email: landscapesuicideproductions@gmail.com.
items._genre: experimental electronic / noise / power electronics / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这是一张在噪音与电子之间寻找中间地带的卡带作品。作者将截获信号般的扭曲波动与模拟反馈的尖啸作为结构骨架，采用自由即兴式推进，留出充足的呼吸空间。A面以受伤而几乎不可辨的人声逐渐让位于高频切片与振荡静电，峰值段落如同磁带即将烧穿般激烈失控。B面则转向沉思与脆弱的简约美学，终曲切入人声呐喊，在小调和声的底层上呈现哀悼式的宣泄。评论指出作品若缩减时长或将更为凝练，但其创意密度与情感浓度足以支撑反复聆听。整体展现出实验声响设计中罕见的方向感与执行力。

items.body: “Some endings don’t wait They arrive before you do” There is a peculiar humiliation in realizing that a relationship has ended while you were still making plans for it. Familiar routines can keep the illusion going for weeks: another message, another evening together, another promise you have learned to accept without examining too closely. Then some ordinary detail makes the situation impossible to explain away, and you find yourself catching up with a loss that has already happened. It’s the emotional equivalent of arriving late to a funeral party: the bar is empty, and the deviled eggs are already gone, and yet you’re still expecting the deceased to call you back. That liminal stretch between an ending and the moment you finally recognize it is the pulse of “No Flowers in June,” the latest single from Italian darkwave duo Soft Scent. A frantic bassline drives relentlessly onward as the synths press in around it, giving the track the jittery resolve of someone who’s just realized that standing still may be the worst thing to do. Moving on takes effort—especially when some part of you is still waiting for the other person to show up. Anna “MissLucifer” and Sara “Felina Noir” formed Soft Scent in 2023 in Italy’s Marche region, and the track is the first single from their forthcoming second album, Mother’s Ruin. Its restless movement draws on coldwave, old EBM, post-punk, the clipped propulsion of punk, and a glossy electronic abrasion that keeps the familiar ingredients feeling unsettled. At odd moments, the song seems to sit somewhere between Björk and Sigue Sigue Sputnik, which sounds ridiculous until you hear the vocal drama and synthetic sleaze brushing past one another. The song is about an ending, although not one of those glamorous endings rock music usually prefers. Nobody is smashing a mirror or walking dramatically into traffic. This is the more common variety: the thing is already over, and you are late to your own realization. Soft Scent refuses to overplay the tragedy. The arrangement holds its dark-disco poise: the bass stays restless, the electronics keep the pressure on. The hurt is unmistakable, but the song never crumples theatrically to make its point. That restraint cuts deeper than a dozen grand breakdowns ever could. The song’s video sets the band on a shadow-drenched stage, purple light pooling around them as candles and flowers frame the scene. It might have slipped into goth by numbers, but something stranger stirs—especially beside the album’s dried and ceramic blooms, and its Victorian Lover’s Eye imagery. Romance has survived, it seems, though never unwatched. Watch the video for No Flowers in June below: The title of Soft Scent’s forthcoming second studio album, Mother’s Ruin, comes from the old Victorian name for gin, which gives the album its larger framework: comfort and damage sharing the same glass. “No Flowers in June” fits neatly into that idea because it concerns the moment after escape has stopped working. You get your temporary relief, your little private holiday from consequence, and eventually consequence finds the forwarding address. No Flowers In June was recorded with Gianluca Lo Presti and mixed and mastered by William Faith, and thankfully nobody has polished it into sterility. It still has elbows. It still has that slightly unfriendly quality good dark music ought to possess. Soft Scent are not reinventing darkwave here, and that is probably beside the point. They are doing something more difficult. They are making it sound like it still has somewhere to go. Mother’s Ruin is expected in late 2026. In the meantime, order No Flowers in June here. items._cn_summary: Soft Scent这首新单以关系结束后迟来的醒悟为核心意象，拒绝夸张煽情，转而用持续推进的低音线、压迫感合成器与紧张的人声表现停滞和走出困境所需的努力。编曲融合冷潮、老派电子舞曲、朋克与暗黑迪斯科元素，在熟悉 ingredients 中保留不安感，既有类型辨识度，也具备一定的声音层次。乐队来自意大利马尔凯，MV以紫色灯光、蜡烛和干花营造阴郁仪式感；作品同时预示了第二张专辑《Mother’s Ruin》对慰藉与损伤并存的叙事关注。

items.body: Reading back into the reviews of this recording, from over the past decades, you encounter the word “relentless” a lot, probably more than for any other album in the history of albums. It’s interesting because, when I first heard Interstellar Space , “relentless” was the word that occurred to me — right after the introductory bells of track one faded. Till then, I hadn’t realized that “relentless” was a thing that music could be, and that relentlessness was awesome. Even transcendent. It’s not a complicated record. You’ve got your tenor and drums. Each piece starts with a theme, enters the improvisation, and then winds down and restates the theme. Each improvisation travels a similar arc, beginning in a saner space, rising intensity and ecstasy, whipping us into a frenzy, then easing off into … well, not serenity, but you get close to it as you hear the shaken bells that begin the next piece. The joys of Interstellar Space come not from structural intrigue, but from the cascadingly brilliant improvs. Coltrane and Ali were both ridiculously ON that day. (Ali actually felt he had underperformed because he didn’t know they were doing a duet session until he arrived at the session.) And the duet setting makes the music almost transparent. Aside from the beauty of Trane and Ali’s playing, you also get a sense of exactly what Coltrane was trying for. His insistent explorations (relentless) are laid bare. This is an excellent entry to Coltrane’s later works. His playing is like water moving through the ground, trying to find its way through a shelf of granite. Eventually, the water finds the crevices, freezes, expands, thaws, and breaks the stone to pieces. The water always wins. A force of nature. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑仅由次中音萨克斯与鼓构成二重奏结构，是约翰·柯川晚期最具实验性的录音之一。每首曲目遵循相似弧线：以简短主题开场，随即进入即兴段，强度逐步攀升至狂喜与亢奋的顶点，最后回落并以铃声衔接下一段。评论特别指出，柯川与鼓手拉希德·阿里当天的演奏状态极为出色，双重奏的极简编制让音乐几近透明，柯川持续探索的精神被完全裸露呈现。评论以水的意象作比喻——柯川的演奏如水穿石，经过冰冻、膨胀、消融的循环，最终将花岗岩击碎。专辑不依赖复杂结构取胜，而以层层递进、不断翻涌的即兴段落为核心，展现了一种接近超验的音乐力量。

Contemporary musicians have been invited to re-score existing film pieces, with the purpose of bringing into the limelight lost or otherwise forgotten works and presenting different artistic takes on the film. items.body: Phantom Limb’s soundtrack imprint Geist im Kino is launching a new series entitled Imaginal Soundtracking on June 19. Contemporary musicians have been invited to re-score existing film pieces, with the purpose of bringing into the limelight lost or otherwise forgotten works and presenting different artistic takes on the film. In this edition, a quartet takes on the award-winning animation There Will Come Soft Rains, a 1984 film by Nazim Tulvakhodzayev which was based on the short story by Ray Bradbury, which in turn refers to a 1918 poem by Sara Teasdale, in which mankind is threatened by war. The poem also speaks of nature’s resilience, thriving once again after destruction, and after our last footsteps have been erased. Despite being written over a century ago, the poem has more than a sliver of significance in the modern era, and its ongoing relevance is quite a shock to the system. Masaaki Yoshida constructs his piece around a lonely piano and a steady metronomic click, retaining the original voice of the robot in the film to send the piece back in time and to give it a padding of authenticity, while gentle chords revolve around it, flowing freely and in stark contrast to a robot’s mechanical stutters. Quiet, sombre, and touching, the piece reflects on and walks among the debris, devastation, and stillness after a nuclear holocaust; some kind of peace even in the death of things. Lakker, Rully Shabara, and Dylan Henner bring their compositions to the record, too, but perhaps the most striking aspect of There Will Come Soft Rains is the diversity on offer, as well as the differing interpretations from the respective artists. Even though it’s the same film, the musicians have provided their own individual takes and thoughts. Electronic duo Lakker inject the music with venomous synths and complex layering which sync up with the climax of the film. Rully Shabara is the vocalist for the experimental Indonesian duo, Senyawa, and his interpretation is sculpted from a bedrock of drone and unique vocal arrangements. Dylan Henner’s track is also surprising, rephrasing and rearranging the robot’s voice until it represents something more malevolent and devilish, and the music never escapes from its doom-like feeling, which is just the kind of harmonic Imaginal Soundtracking Vol. 1: There Will Come Soft Rains was looking to hit. Imaginal Soundtracking 1: There Will Come Soft Rains by Masaaki Yoshida, Lakker, Rully Shabara, Dylan Henner www.phantomlimblabel.bandcamp.com
items._genre: experimental electronic / drone / ambient / sound art / film score
items._cn_summary: Phantom Limb旗下Geist im Kino厂牌推出Imaginal Soundtracking系列，邀请当代音乐人为被遗忘的影像作品重新配乐。首卷以1984年Nazim Tulvakhodzayev改编自Ray Bradbury同名小说的动画短片为蓝本，收录四位音乐人的独立诠释。Masaaki Yoshida以孤寂钢琴与节拍器滴答声为骨架，保留原片机器人旁白以增强历史质感，柔和和弦在机械断续声之间自由流淌，营造核战后的废墟沉思。Lakker以毒性合成器与复杂层次推进影片高潮段落。Senyawa主唱Rully Shabara以人声实验与无人机音墙构建作品骨架。Henner则将机器人语音重新处理为更趋邪恶的音色，笼罩于末日般的压迫氛围中。专辑在统一主题下展现截然不同的艺术视角与声响逻辑，四位音乐人的诠释既彼此独立又相互呼应。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. items._cn_summary: 普利姆四重奏联合多位客座音乐家，发布十首作品的专辑《Generate Music》，探索非裔与犹太裔美国人在历史、文化与创作上的联结。四位萨克斯演奏者横跨女高、中音、高音与上低音区，配以电吉他、克拉兹默单簧管、爵士鼓、贝斯、小提琴与诗文念白，构建出融合现代爵士即兴、犹太传统旋律与西非格里奥叙事传统的跨界声场。Ursula Rucker以充满戏剧张力的声音叙述一九六四年民权运动者被害事件，质问听者是否真正关心历史真相。Tyshawn Sorey的鼓击翻腾环绕，David Gilmore的多段炽热吉他独奏与萨克斯四重奏形成自由爵士式的对峙，克拉兹默片段在funk节奏中无缝切入。整体作品以历史反思为骨架，以多元文化对话为肌理，呈现出兼具政治自觉与实验精神的声音叙事。

items.body: Echo �it could be named for the Greek goddess who lost her voice, just as Chandra has lost hers to illness. Or more prosaically, it could be the memories of past performances. Whatever the inspiration, Chandra has said that this is very likely her final album. What a stupendous way to bow out. Echo by Sheila Chandra For someone who spent the first several years of her career as purely a studio artist, she proved herself to be more than adventurous when she took to the stage. Not just for the beauty of her singing, although that�s in evidence throughout, but for the surprises she could pull, as in the three hugely demanding �Speaking In Tongues� pieces here, where the relentless pace as she imitates the percussive patterns of the tablas are enough to cause whiplash. For many it was their introduction to konnokol , most often a way of teaching the rhythms, but more than powerful enough to stand alone. Live performance proved to be a reinvention for her, completely alone on stage, and the trio of albums she recorded exploring drones gave the chance to showcase her imagination and talent, the world of a pioneering artist with an individual vision. It was far from her beginnings in the early 1980s, although she revisits that teenage self on �Ever So Lonely/ Eyes/ Ocean,� transforming a pioneering Anglo-Asian pop fusion into a breathless spiritual experience. Echo by Sheila Chandra As a singer, Chandra was one to quick to spot the similarities between musical cultures, evidenced here in �Lament Of McCrimmon/ Songs of the Banshee,� where her voice soars over the subtle, grounding anchor of the drone to connect the Scottish Highland with the Indian subcontinent. It�s a lush reminder of how delicious Chandra�s singing voice was, and how much poorer the world is now medical problems have robbed us of it. For her, solo truly did mean solo � no band to back her and fill out the sound - and that produced inevitable challenges. Yet nothing here sounds empty or incomplete. The drone gave all she needed, while her vocal lines wrapped around the listener. Echo by Sheila Chandra The final track here, �The Blacksmith� was one she performed with the Imagined Village tour in 2007, making for a solemn, sad parting from the stage. Her final performances came in 2011. For those who never had the chance to see Sheila Chandra perform live, a small figure alone, commanding any stage, this is the next-best thing, with excellent sound quality and her towering presence. It�s an experience to cherish over and over. Chandra has reinvented herself again ( check her website ), but the Echo of her voice will reverberate for many years to come. Find the artist online. Listen to tracks from from the 2023 reissues of Chandra's first solo albums (Review) Ever So Lonely , Chandra's RootsWorld interview from 2022 Sheila Chandra - Live at World In The Park 1992)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Sheila Chandra因疾病失声后的告别之作，以现场录音形式记录了她独居舞台的演绎方式。乐评指出她在三首《Speaking In Tongues》中模仿塔布拉鼓的节奏型，展现了南印度卡诺克尔节奏体系的纯粹声乐运用。专辑核心围绕持续低音（drone）展开，她的人声在其上盘旋缠绕，构建出沉浸式的聆听体验。《Lament Of McCrimmon/ Songs of the Banshee》一曲将苏格兰高地传统与印度次大陆音乐通过人声与低音相连，体现了她对跨文化音乐共性的敏锐嗅觉。另一曲《Ever So Lonely/ Eyes/ Ocean》将早年的盎格鲁-亚洲流行融合重新演绎为精神性的体验。终曲《The Blacksmith》源自2007年Imagined Village巡演，作为舞台告别带有庄严悲悯的色彩。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生的肯尼亚鼓手Sven Kacirek与83岁的传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo及Oluoch兄弟中的Olith Ratengo共同录制。Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手掌打击乐与鼓组构成了器乐基底，与Nengo传承的dodo传统唱法相互呼应，两人因住地相近而形成自然的人声对话。乐评以《Bara》为例，指出层叠的合成多节奏逐步浮现，最终呈现出仿佛一直潜藏于人声之下的有机整体感；《Sarah》中Kacirek的打击与Ratengo的人声在尖锐失真突然介入时形成强烈张力。整篇评论将Palagoma置于Chouk Bwa、Nyege Nyege厂牌等跨文化实验场景中，强调不同文化在回应彼此时不践踏传统，而是让根源走向前卫，让创新看似古老。
